Motivation

This project was motivated by the urgent need to understand and address the silent epidemic of female suicides in India — a deeply gendered public health crisis that remains inadequately studied in quantitative terms.

As students of STA 202: Mathematical Statistics, we recognized that statistical tools — regression modeling, correlation analysis, and exploratory data analysis — are not merely abstract academic exercises, but powerful instruments for illuminating real-world social problems. The NCRB dataset offered a rare opportunity to apply these techniques to a socially significant and underexplored question.

Why Female Suicides?

While national suicide statistics are periodically reported in the media, the specific vulnerabilities of women — rooted in structural inequalities, economic dependency, marital and family pressures, and limited access to mental healthcare — rarely receive focused analytical attention. We wanted to move beyond surface-level reporting and use data to uncover the structural determinants driving this trend.

Why This Dataset?

The NCRB's Accidental Deaths & Suicides in India (ADSI) report is one of the most systematically maintained government datasets on suicide in the country. Its granularity across causes, profession, age groups, and states over a 10-year window provides a unique foundation for longitudinal and multivariate analysis — exactly the kind of challenge suited to our coursework in mathematical statistics.

What We Hoped to Achieve

Academic Goal

Apply regression modeling, hypothesis testing, and correlation techniques from STA 202 to a real-world, high-dimensional dataset — interpreting coefficients, assessing significance, and drawing valid conclusions from limited sample sizes.

Social Goal

Produce evidence-based insights that could inform policymakers, mental health advocates, and public health researchers about which population groups and causes demand the most urgent attention in female suicide prevention.

This project reaffirmed our belief that statistics, when applied with rigour and empathy, can be a tool for social good. The numbers in this report represent real lives — and understanding them is the first step towards change.

1. Introduction

Suicide is a major public health crisis in India — the world's most populous country — claiming over 130,000 lives each year. Female suicides, accounting for approximately 32% of all suicides, reveal unique socio-demographic vulnerabilities shaped by gender roles, economic dependency, marital norms, and mental health barriers.

This report presents a rigorous statistical examination of female suicide patterns in India over a decade (2014–2023) using data from the National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB), the authoritative government agency responsible for collecting and publishing crime and accidental death statistics.

Female suicides in India are structurally different from male suicides: they are disproportionately concentrated among housewives, are more strongly linked to family and marriage-related stressors, and exhibit distinct geographic clustering. Understanding the factors that drive these numbers — through statistical modeling — is essential for designing effective intervention strategies.

This study employs multiple regression techniques to identify the strongest predictors of female suicide counts at the national level, supported by exploratory visualizations, correlation analysis, and state-level comparison.

2. Objectives

The primary and secondary objectives of this study are:

Primary Objective

To build and evaluate regression models that identify statistically significant predictors of female suicide counts in India using cause, profession, and temporal variables from NCRB data.

Secondary Objectives
  • Analyze national trends in female suicides (2014–2023)
  • Identify high-risk states and demographic groups
  • Examine the distribution across causes and professions
  • Assess correlation structure among suicide determinants
  • Interpret coefficient directions and significance levels

3. Data Description

All data used in this study originates exclusively from the National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB), Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India — specifically from their annual publication "Accidental Deaths & Suicides in India" (ADSI) for the years 2014 through 2023.

3.1 Dataset Files

8 structured CSV files were used:
  • ncrb_female_suicides_MASTER.csv — 354 rows: State × Year panel with region classification
  • ncrb_female_suicides_allindia_summary.csv — 10 rows: National aggregates (male, female, total) per year
  • ncrb_female_suicides_causewise.csv — 300 rows: 30 cause categories × 10 years
  • ncrb_female_suicides_professionwise.csv — 99 rows: 11 profession categories × 10 years (some missing)
  • ncrb_female_suicides_statewise.csv — 360 rows: State × Year
  • ncrb_female_suicides_wide.csv — 38 rows: Wide format (states as rows, years as columns)
  • ncrb_statewise_cause_female.csv — 10,437 rows: State × Year × Cause granular data
  • ncrb_statewise_profession_female.csv — 8,280 rows: State × Year × Profession granular data

3.2 Key Variables

Dependent Variable:
  • Female_Suicides (annual national count)

Cause Variables (30 categories):
  • Family Problems, Illness (Total), Love Affairs
  • Marriage Related Issues, Failure in Examination
  • Bankruptcy/Indebtedness, Other Causes
  • Drug Abuse, Physical Abuse (Rape), Poverty, etc.
Profession Variables (11 categories):
  • Housewife (dominant category)
  • Students, Unemployed Persons
  • Daily Wage Earner, Self-employed
  • Agricultural Labourers, Farmers/Cultivators

Temporal & Geographic:
  • Year (2014–2023)
  • State_UT (38 states/UTs)
  • Region (East/West/North/South/Central)

4. Methodology

4.1 Analytical Framework

The study follows a sequential analytical pipeline: (1) data loading and cleaning, (2) exploratory data analysis and visualization, (3) Pearson correlation screening for feature selection, (4) multiple ordinary least squares (OLS) regression modeling, and (5) model comparison and interpretation.

4.2 Regression Model Specification

Five regression models were specified and estimated:

Model 1 — Temporal Trend

Simple regression of Female Suicides on Year alone, to establish baseline temporal dynamics.

Female_Suicides = β₀ + β₁·Year + ε
Model 2 — Cause-Based Model

Multiple regression using 7 key cause categories as predictors.

Female_Suicides = β₀ + β₁·FamilyProblems + β₂·Illness + β₃·LoveAffairs + β₄·MarriageIssues + β₅·ExamFailure + β₆·Bankruptcy + β₇·OtherCauses + ε
Model 3 — Profession-Based Model

Multiple regression using 8 profession categories (Housewife, Students, Unemployed, Daily Wage Earner, etc.).

Model 4 — Full Saturated Model

Combines Year, all cause, and all profession variables. Results in a perfectly-fit but overparameterized model (n=10, k=16), rendering standard errors unreliable due to near-perfect multicollinearity.

Model 5 — Parsimonious Model (Significant Predictors)

Retains only variables with Pearson |r| significant at p<0.05: Illness_Total, Housewife, Students, Year, Love_Affairs, Farmers_Cultivators, Bankruptcy, Family_Problems.

4.3 Statistical Methods

All regression coefficients were estimated using the ordinary least squares (OLS) criterion (minimizing sum of squared residuals). Standard errors were derived from the inverse of the information matrix (X'X)⁻¹ · MSE. t-statistics were computed as β/SE(β), and two-tailed p-values were obtained from the t-distribution with (n−k−1) degrees of freedom. The F-statistic tests the joint significance of all predictors. Model performance was evaluated using R² and adjusted R² (which penalizes for additional predictors).

4.4 Feature Selection

Given the small sample size (n=10 years at national level), multivariate models are prone to overfitting. A Pearson correlation screen was applied to all candidate predictors. Only features with statistically significant bivariate correlations (p<0.05) were retained in the parsimonious Model 5.

⚠️ Important Statistical Note:

With only 10 observations (years) at national level, all regression models have limited degrees of freedom. Models with many predictors (Models 3–5) must be interpreted with caution — high R² values in small samples are prone to overfitting. The Pearson correlation table and Model 2 (with fewer predictors) provide the most reliable inferential guidance.

5. Exploratory Data Analysis

5.1 National Trend: Female vs Male Suicides

The figure below illustrates the total annual suicide counts broken down by gender from 2014 to 2023. Female suicides have maintained a relatively stable share of about 32% of total suicides, but have shown a noticeable upward trend since 2020, reaching the highest recorded level of 53,082 in 2023 — a 24.8% increase over the 2014 baseline of 42,521.

Key Finding:

Female suicides declined slightly from 2014–2018, then rose sharply from 2019 onwards. The 2020–2023 period shows the steepest increase, likely influenced by pandemic-related stressors, economic disruption, and reporting normalization.

5.2 Year-over-Year Change

The year-over-year analysis reveals that female suicides declined in 2015 and 2016, remained relatively flat through 2018, then increased steadily from 2019. The largest single-year absolute increase occurred between 2022 and 2023 (+3,543 cases, +7.2%).

5.3 State-Level Analysis: High-Risk States

Geographic concentration is stark. Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Madhya Pradesh, West Bengal, and Telangana account for the largest cumulative female suicide counts across the decade. These five states collectively account for over 45% of all female suicides in India. Southern and western states consistently report higher absolute numbers, partly reflecting population size and potentially better reporting compliance.

State Trend Note:

Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu show consistent high numbers across all 10 years. Telangana, newly formed in 2014, shows rapidly increasing counts. Several northeastern and small UTs show very low counts but may have structural underreporting issues.

5.4 Cause Analysis

The cause-wise breakdown reveals that Family Problems and Illness (including mental illness) are the two dominant cause categories, together accounting for the majority of female suicides. Marriage-related issues (dowry, extra-marital affairs, non-settlement) represent a significant cluster specific to the female population.

Cause Hierarchy (National Cumulative 2014–2023):

1st: Other Causes / Family Problems · 2nd: Illness (Total) · 3rd: Love Affairs · 4th: Marriage Related Issues · 5th: Other Prolonged Illness · 6th: Failure in Examination

5.5 Profession Analysis

The profession breakdown is one of the most striking findings in the dataset. Housewives account for approximately 45–47% of all female suicides every year — a persistently dominant share that reflects the economic dependency, social isolation, and household stress experienced by homemakers in India. Students and daily wage earners are the next most affected groups.

Key Finding:

Housewife suicides show a clear upward trend since 2018, while student suicides have increased sharply after 2020. This temporal divergence suggests different underlying drivers — domestic stress for housewives, and academic/employment anxiety for students.

5.6 Correlation Structure

The correlation heatmap among cause variables reveals strong positive co-movement among illness-related causes (Cancer, Paralysis, Insanity/Mental Illness), suggesting these are co-occurring risk factors. Family-problem causes also cluster together. Negative correlations appear between some economic causes (Unemployment, Property Dispute) and certain social causes.

Despite retaining only significant bivariate predictors, the multivariate model's overall F-test is not significant (p=0.474). This is a classic case of multicollinearity and overfitting with n=10: all predictors correlate highly with each other AND with the dependent variable, so the unique marginal contribution of each predictor is inflated standard errors. The bivariate results (Model 1 and Pearson table) remain the most reliable inferential outputs.

7.2 Key Findings from Regression

Finding 1: Illness is the Strongest Predictor

Illness_Total has the highest Pearson correlation (r=0.909***) with female suicides. In Model 2, its coefficient (β=1.52) indicates that for every additional illness-related female suicide, approximately 1.5 more female suicides are expected on average across other categories — reflecting a deep co-movement between health vulnerability and overall female suicide burden.

Finding 2: Housewife Status is a Structural Driver

Housewife suicides have one of the strongest correlations with total female suicides (r=0.853**). With β=2.43 in Model 3, housewife suicides are the dominant professional category. This underlines how domestic roles, economic powerlessness, and intimate partner violence create concentrated suicide risk among homemakers.

Finding 3: Rising Student Suicides — A New Trend

Student suicides (r=0.849**) show strong positive correlation and an accelerating post-2020 trend. The post-pandemic environment of disrupted academic careers, examination pressure, and social isolation appears to have significantly elevated student suicide risk.

Finding 4: Time Trend is Significant (p=0.006)

Year is a significant predictor (β=635.85, p=0.006) indicating a structural upward trend of approximately 636 additional female suicides per year, after controlling for nothing else. This secular increase signals a worsening crisis requiring systemic intervention.

Finding 5: Farming Community Shows Negative Association

Farmers_Cultivators shows a significant negative correlation (r=−0.730*) with total female suicides. This may reflect compositional shifts over time — as the agricultural workforce feminizes or contracts — rather than a protective effect per se.

Finding 6: Cause Model Dominates

Model 2 (Causes) achieves the best balance of fit and significance (R²=0.986, Adj-R²=0.936, F-test p=0.049). The coefficients of Family_Problems (β=1.67) and Illness_Total (β=1.52) are the largest positive predictors, confirming these as the two primary cause-based drivers of female suicide counts in India.

8. Discussion

8.1 Socio-Demographic Patterns

The overwhelming concentration of female suicides among housewives (~46%) reflects a deeply gendered vulnerability in Indian society. Housewives in India often lack independent income, have limited access to social support outside the home, and face significantly higher risks from domestic violence and marital discord. The NCRB data consistently places "Family Problems" as the leading reported cause, which resonates with this structural interpretation.

The sharp post-2020 increase in student suicides — visible in the trend plots — corresponds with the COVID-19 pandemic's disruption of educational institutions, cancelled examinations, and the shift to online learning that increased social isolation. The academic pressure that has historically driven male student suicides in India appears to have intensified for female students as well, particularly in competitive examination contexts.

8.2 Geographic Concentration

The state-level heatmap reveals that Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, and Madhya Pradesh are persistently high across the decade. This is partly a function of population size, but relative rates (per 100,000 women) tell a more nuanced story. Southern states (Tamil Nadu, Telangana, Karnataka) show higher absolute counts but also have generally higher reporting fidelity. The Northeastern states show very low absolute numbers that may reflect underreporting as much as lower actual rates.

8.3 Regression Model Interpretation

The finding that cause-based variables explain 98.6% of variance in female suicide counts (R²=0.986 in Model 2) while maintaining overall significance (F=19.92, p=0.049) validates the importance of understanding the why behind suicide statistics. The structural co-movement between illness categories and the overall female suicide count suggests that mental health disorders, chronic illness, and the stigma around seeking treatment create a compounding risk pathway.

The significant time trend (β≈636/year, p=0.006) indicates that structural factors — urbanization stress, economic pressure, social media influence on mental health, increasing awareness-and-reporting — are driving a long-run upward trend that is unlikely to self-correct without policy intervention.

8.4 High-Risk Groups Identified

Highest Risk Demographic Profile:
  • Housewives aged 18–40
  • Residents of Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, MP, West Bengal
  • Causes: Family problems, marital discord
  • Economic dependency and low social capital
Emerging Risk Group:
  • Female students (15–25 age band)
  • Post-2020 acceleration in trend
  • Exam failure, academic pressure, social isolation
  • Urban and semi-urban concentration likely

9. Limitations

1. Small Sample Size for Regression:

With only 10 annual observations at the national level, all multivariate regression models suffer from limited degrees of freedom. This leads to inflated R² values and unreliable individual coefficient significance even when the overall model is significant. Results should be interpreted directionally rather than as precise estimates.

2. Multicollinearity:

Cause categories and profession categories are highly intercorrelated (they measure aspects of the same underlying phenomenon). This makes it difficult to isolate the independent contribution of any single variable. VIF (Variance Inflation Factor) analysis was not performed due to the singular matrix issue in saturated models.

3. Ecological Fallacy Risk:

All regression was conducted at the national aggregate level (10 observations). Inferences about individual-level risk factors from aggregate-level associations are subject to the ecological fallacy. State-level panel regression (n=380) would provide more reliable estimates but requires additional data harmonization.

4. Reporting Heterogeneity:

NCRB data relies on police-recorded deaths. Suicides in India are substantially underreported — particularly in rural areas and among communities with social stigma around suicide. The data reflects reported suicides, not true incidence. Quality of reporting varies across states and years.

5. Missing Socioeconomic Controls:

Variables such as per capita income, female literacy rate, gender parity index, access to mental healthcare, and divorce rates are not present in the NCRB dataset. Regression models omit these potentially important confounders.

6. Classification Changes:

The NCRB occasionally revises cause and profession classification schemas between years. Some categories in earlier years do not map exactly to later categories, which may introduce minor inconsistencies in time-series analysis.

10. Conclusion

This study presents the most comprehensive statistical and regression analysis of female suicides in India (2014–2023) using NCRB data across 38 states and Union Territories.

The analysis reveals five core conclusions:

  1. Upward Secular Trend: Female suicides have increased at a statistically significant rate of approximately 636 per year nationally (p=0.006), with the steepest acceleration occurring after 2020.
  2. Illness and Family Problems Dominate: The cause-based regression model (R²=0.986, p=0.049) confirms that illness-related and family-problem causes are the two strongest predictors of annual female suicide counts.
  3. Housewives Remain Disproportionately Affected: At ~46% of all female suicides, housewives represent the single most at-risk occupational group — an enduring structural inequality reflecting economic dependency and domestic vulnerability.
  4. Student Suicides are an Emerging Crisis: Post-2020 trend acceleration among students, combined with a strong positive correlation (r=0.849) with aggregate female suicides, signals a growing mental health emergency in the education sector.
  5. Geographic Concentration Demands Targeted Policy: Five states (Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Madhya Pradesh, West Bengal, Telangana) account for over 45% of cumulative female suicides and should be prioritized in state-level mental health interventions.
Policy Implications:

These findings call for gender-sensitive mental health programs specifically targeting housewives through community health workers and frontline services. Academic stress reduction programs and counselling infrastructure in schools and colleges are urgently needed. State-level mental health authorities in Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, and Madhya Pradesh should receive enhanced resources and monitoring. Illness-linked suicide prevention — bridging physical healthcare with psychological support — represents a major opportunity for systemic intervention.

Future research should expand this analysis using state-level panel regression (n≈380) with additional socioeconomic covariates, incorporate suicide attempt data where available, and explore Poisson or Negative Binomial models better suited to count outcomes.
